Oncology is the branch of medicine concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. Mathematical models can be used to study how cancer develops, grows, and spreads. By providing quantitative and predictive frameworks, mathematical models allow hypotheses about cancer to be tested and evaluated. A carcinogen is any substance that causes cancer. Carcinogenesis is the process by which normal cells are transformed into cancer cells. A key observation that motivated many mathematical models of carcinogenesis is cancer incidence. Cancer incidence often increases rapidly with age, while the occurrence of cancer in an individual appears highly stochastic. However, patterns emerge when cancer incidence is examined across populations. These observations contributed to the development of multistage theories of carcinogenesis, which describe cancer development as a sequence of stages or changes in cells. Beginning in the 1920s, experiments involving chemical carcinogens provided evidence for the idea that cancer develops through multiple stages. In particular, applying two different carcinogens in sequence often produced higher cancer rates than applying a single carcinogen over time, leading to the two-stage model of carcinogenesis. Charles and Luce-Clausen developed one of the first quantitative multistage theories in the 1940s, using a mathematical model to describe the development of skin tumors in mice. Their work demonstrated how mathematical models could be used to connect assumptions about cellular changes with observed cancer incidence. Armitage and Doll further developed multistage theory in the 1950s, introducing more general mathematical models that allowed different rates for different stages and treated the stages as sequential cellular changes rather than necessarily genetic mutations. Their work helped establish mathematical modelling as a framework for studying the development of cancer. 2.3 What is a Mathematical Model? A mathematical model is a numerical representation of a real-world problem. By replacing physical experimentation with mathematical simulations, it allows researchers to evaluate system dynamics and predict future outcomes. 2.4 Systems of ODEs as Mathematical Models A system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) is a set of equations that involves two or more dependent variables that depend on one independent variable. A solution to this system is a set of functions that satisfies each equation on some interval \(I\). A system of ODEs can serve as a mathematical model by describing real world systems where multiple interacting components evolve over a shared independent variable. For example, in ecology, the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model uses a system of two coupled ODEs to track the interdependent population sizes of two interacting species over time \(t\). Many mathematical models are described using systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). It is useful to identify equilibrium points of a system of ODEs and study the stability of the equilibria. Consider the following system of ODEs: \[ rac{dx}{dt} = f(x,y)\] \[ rac{dy}{dt} = g(x,y)\] 2.5 Review of Mathematical Concepts 2.5.1 The Characteristic Equation For a square matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n 	imes n}\), the characteristic equation is given by \(\det(A - \lambda I) = 0\). This yields an \(n\)-degree polynomial whose roots correspond directly to the matrix’s eigenvalues \(\lambda\). 2.5.2 The Jacobian Matrix For a vector-valued function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R}^m\) given by \(f(x) = (f_1(x), \dots, f_m(x))\) where \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\), the Jacobian matrix \(J\) is the \(m 	imes n\) matrix of first-order partial derivatives: \[J =  egin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_n} \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ \dfrac{\partial f_m}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \dfrac{\partial f_m}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix}\] When \(m=n\), i.e., the matrix is square, its determinant, commonly referred to as the Jacobian, acts as a local scaling factor. The Jacobian plays an essential role in coordinate transformations by describing how areas or volumes stretch, rotate, and distort under a change of variables. Consider the system of ODEs above. The Jacobian matrix of the system is \[J(x,y)=  egin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\ \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix}\] This matrix contains the first order partial derivatives of \(f\) and \(g\), describing how small changes in \(x\) and \(y\) affect the rate of change of the system. 2.5.3 Equilibrium Points and Local Stability An equilibrium point is a point \((x^*, y^*)\) such that \( rac{dx}{dt} = 0\) and \( rac{dy}{dt} = 0\). That is, an equilibrium point is a point at which both variables \(x\) and \(y\) remain constant over time. At an equilibrium, there is no net change in either variable. It is important to note that the equilibrium of a system does not mean that individual processes affecting \(x\) and \(y\) have stopped. Rather, the processes are balancing each other. Finding an equilibrium tells us where a system can remain unchanged, but does not tell us what happens if the system is slightly disturbed. Stability describes how a system behaves following a small deviation from an equilibrium. An equilibrium is stable if solutions that start sufficiently close to the equilibrium remain close to it. An equilibrium is asymptotically stable, if it is stable and solutions that start sufficiently close will eventually approach the equilibrium. An equilibrium is unstable if it is not stable. To study the local stability of an equilibrium \((x^*, y^*)\), we analyse the eigenvalues of \(J(x^*, y^*)\). Let \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) be eigenvalues of \(J(x^*, y^*)\), and \((x^*, y^*)\) an equilibrium point. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both real and negative, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is asymptotically stable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both real and positive, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is unstable. If \(\lambda _ 1 < 0\) and \(\lambda_2 > 0\), with both being real, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is called a saddle point and is unstable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both complex with negative real parts, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is asymptotically stable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both complex with positive real parts, then \((x^*, y^*)\) is unstable. If \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are both purely imaginary, then the linearized system exhibits oscillatory behaviour. Further analysis is required to determine stability. Firstly, the activation term \(\alpha\) is simplistic and does not capture the complexities of immune responses to tumour growth. Chapter 3 The Kuznetsov Tumour–Immune Model 3.1 The Simple Kuznetsov Model A tumour is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide more than they should or do not die when they should. Tumours may be benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer). Malignant tumours can spread into, or invade, nearby tissues. They can also spread to other parts of the body through the blood and lymph systems. Tumour cells reproduce and therefore could increase the tumour population. Moreover, tumour cells can also be removed through interactions with immune effector cells. These cells recognize and respond to abnormal cells, including tumour cells. Some examples of these cells are cytotoxic T lymphocytes and natural killer cells. Define the following: \(E\): Number of effector cells located at the tumor site, \(T\): Number of tumor cells located at the tumor site, \(s\): Baseline rate at which mature effector cells enter the tumour region, \(p\): Rate of tumour stimulated effector cell accumulation \(g\): Saturation parameter for tumour stimulated effector cell accumulation, \(m\): Rate of effector cell inactivation due to interactions with tumour cells, \(n\): Rate of tumour cell killing through interactions with effector cells, \(d\): Rate of ordinary effector cell elimination \(a\): Maximum growth rate of the tumor cell population, \(b\): Inverse of maximum carrying capacity, where all of the above parameters are positive. To determine the rate of change of the effector cell population, we consider processes that increase and decrease the number of effector cells. Effector cells enter the tumour region at baseline rate \(s\). Tumour cells also stimulate the accumulation of effector cells. We assume that this stimulation increases with tumour cell number but eventually saturates, giving the term \( rac{pET}{g+T}\). The saturation reflects the assumption that the accumulation of effector cells cannot increase indefinitely as tumour size increases, due to biological limitations. Effector cells are also inactivated through interactions with tumour cells at a rate proportional to both \(E\) and \(T\), giving the term \(mET\). Finally, effector cells are eliminated naturally at a rate proportional to the size of the population, giving the term \(dE\). Rather than solving the cubic directly, we can bound – and in this case pin down – the number of positive roots purely from the signs of its coefficients, using Descartes’ Rule of Signs: the number of positive real roots of a real polynomial is either equal to the number of sign changes in its ordered coefficient sequence, or less than that by an even number. Step 1: Sign of \(C_3\). Since \(m,b>0\), we always have \(C_3 = mb>0\). Step 2: Sign of \(C_0\). Real tumors, however, are heterogeneous, and subclones that partially evade immune-mediated killing are a central driver of treatment failure. As a first extension, we equip the tumor cell population \(T\) with a degree of immune resistance, benchmarked directly against the Kuznetsov model so that setting the resistance parameters to their “no resistance” values recovers Section 3.1 exactly. The model presented here is the single-subpopulation special case of a more general two-subpopulation (immune-resistant vs. immune-sensitive, with optional chemotherapy resistance) model developed in (mokari26?), to which we refer the reader for the full treatment, including both immune-evasion mechanisms considered simultaneously with chemotherapy. We assume resistance carries a growth-rate cost \(\zeta>0\), so the resistant population’s growth rate is \(a_T=a-\zeta\) rather than the wild-type rate \(a\), and confers a benefit \(	heta\in[0,1]\) that reduces the effectiveness of effector-mediated killing (\(	heta=1\) recovers full susceptibility, i.e. no resistance). Writing \(E\) for the effector population and \(\kappa=1/b\) for the carrying capacity, the dynamics are \[ egin{equation}  rac{dT}{dt} = \left(a_T\left(1- rac{T}{\kappa}ight) - 	heta Eight)T, 	ag{3.4} \end{equation}\] \[ egin{equation}  rac{dE}{dt} = \left( rac{p_T T}{T+g} - m_T T - dight)E + s. 	ag{3.5} \end{equation}\] This is structurally identical to (3.1) and (3.2): tumor growth is logistic and suppressed by effector-mediated killing at rate \(	heta E\); effectors are produced at baseline rate \(s\), activated through a saturating term with parameters \(p_T,g\), exhausted or inactivated by the tumor at rate \(m_T\), and die naturally at rate \(d\). However, the qualitative behaviour of the system may change when one or more model parameters are varied. Parameters such as tumour growth rates, immune response strength, and immune evasion may differ between individuals or change over time. Hence, it is important to consider how the model may change when we vary the parameters. A bifurcation occurs when a small change in a parameter causes a qualitative change in the behaviour of a dynamical system. These changes may include the appearance or disappearance of equilibrium points, or a change in the stability of an equilibrium. For the Kuznetsov model, parameters such as the maximum tumour growth rate \(a\), the tumour killing rate \(n\), and the rate of tumour-stimulated effector accumulation \(p\) may be treated as bifurcation parameters. Varying these parameters allows us to study how changes in tumour growth or immune activity affect the equilibria of the system. In particular, the parameter \(	heta\) represents the effectiveness of immune-mediated tumour killing relative to the original tumour population. A decrease in \(	heta\) therefore corresponds to increased immune resistance. By varying \(	heta\), we can examine whether increasing tumour resistance changes the number or stability of the equilibria. Bifurcation diagrams provide information that cannot be obtained from a single phase plane plot. A phase diagram describes the behaviour of the system for one fixed set of parameters, whereas a bifurcation diagram describes how the long term behaviour of the system changes across a range of parameter values. The bifurcation diagrams illustrate how changes in model parameters affect the number and stability of equilibrium points. Figure 3.4 shows the effect of varying the baseline effector cell influx rate \(s\) in the original Kuznetsov model. For smaller values of \(s\), multiple positive equilibria exist, including two stable equilibria separated by an unstable saddle point. As \(s\) increases, some equilibria disappear through a saddle-node bifurcation. This demonstrates how increasing immune effector cells can change the long term behaviour of the tumour–immune system. Figures 3.5 and 3.6 illustrate the effects of immune resistance under reduced antigen presentation and immune checkpoint evasion, respectively. In both cases, \(	heta\) represents the effectiveness of immune-mediated tumour killing, with smaller values corresponding to greater resistance. Under reduced antigen presentation, increasing \(	heta\) can lead to the appearance of additional positive equilibria, while the checkpoint evasion model maintains multiple positive equilibria across the parameter range considered. These results demonstrate that different resistance mechanisms can affect the equilibrium structure differently, even when both reduce the effectiveness of immune-mediated tumour killing. 3.6 Summary Starting from the two-population Kuznetsov tumor–immune model, we showed that its coexistence-equilibrium structure is governed by a cubic polynomial whose coefficient signs – not its explicit roots – determine whether the system is monostable or bistable. The same sign-test machinery, applied unchanged after remapping three parameters to account for a resistant phenotype, shows that an immune-resistant tumor subpopulation inherits the same qualitative bistability whenever effector activation continues to dominate tumor-induced exhaustion at the resistant phenotype’s parameter values. This worked example illustrates a general strategy for analyzing tumor–immune models in this course: reduce the equilibrium condition to a low-degree polynomial, and use a sign test on its coefficients, rather than brute-force root-finding, to characterize the number and type of biologically admissible steady states. % %

Write an introductory agent-based model in R to simulate tumor/immune cell interactions 4.2 Introduction: Why Agent-Based Modeling in Oncology? Agent-based modeling (ABM) is a bottom-up computer simulation technique that models the individual behavior of autonomous units. Agent-based models are particularly powerful in oncology because they account for the variability and heterogeneity of the cells in the body of someone with the disease; they allow scientists to simulate the behaviors of individual cells and observe how they drive tumor growth, therapeutic resistance, and immune evasion. 4.2.1 Comparing Modeling Approaches: ODEs vs. ABMs Compared to traditional models, the computational expense of ABMs is very high since they process autonomous entities (agents) concurrently, and they can range from thousands to millions. Models including agents, however, are rarely purely discrete. In recent years, efforts in integrative science have facilitated iterative collaboration (West et al, 2024) not only to overcome computational limitations, but to accurately model a multi-scale disease. ABMs handle intercellular interactions, mutations, and highly variable events, while differential equations handle continuous variables like nutrients and the spread of chemotherapeutic drugs. In oncology, ABMs are also often integrated with differential equations and machine learning. 4.2.2 When to Use ABMs in Cancer Biology Understanding when to choose an ABM over traditional continuous or aggregate modeling methods is essential for effective computational design. ABMs are best suited for systems with: - High Heterogeneity: The agents of the system are diverse, unique, and possess distinct states, rules, or behaviors (e.g., different cell types in a tissue, cells at varying stages of the cell cycle, tumor subclones competing for space). - High Environmental Influence: Physical space, location, distance, movement, and local neighborhood interactions (e.g., crowding, physical collisions, diffusion gradients, spatial segregation). - Decentralized Control: There is no central controller or master equation dictating the entire system. Macro-level behavior arises from independent, local interactions. - Non-Linear Dynamics and Feedback Loops: The system features complex feedback loops where individual actions change the environment, which in turn alters how individuals behave. 4.3 The Four Pillar Ingredients of an Oncology ABM Ordinary differential equation (ODE) models treat populations as continuous averages. In reality, however, cancer is driven by three factors: individual differences between cells, competition for space, and direct interactions with their surroundings. To capture these biological dynamics in a computer simulation, Agent-Based Models (ABMs) rely on four core building blocks: 4.3.1 Agents and State Variables Agents are independent computational entities representing individual biological actors (for example, tumor cells, cytotoxic T lymphocytes, macrophages, or stromal fibroblasts). Each agent maintains its own internal state variables, which may include: Spatial Coordinates: Position \((x, y)\) on a discrete lattice or continuous coordinate space. Agent Type / Phenotype: Cell lineage (e.g., prey/tumor cell vs. predator/immune cell, stem-like vs. differentiated, sensitive vs. drug-resistant). Internal Resources / Health: Energy level, cell volume, or damage accumulation (e.g., DNA double-strand breaks). Lifecycle Status: Active/proliferating, quiescent, senescent, or flagged for death (apoptotic/necrotic). 4.3.2 Environment (The World) The environment represents the physical tissue domain and biochemical landscape in which agents live: Spatial Topology: Typically presented as a 2D or 3D grid. The boundaries can be reflective (rigid walls) or periodic (wrapping around edges so cells exiting the right re-enter on the left). Physical Exclusion: Rules dictating whether a single lattice site can host multiple agents or enforces volume control (carrying capacity per cell). Background resources: Gradients of extracellular nutrients (glucose, oxygen), chemokines, or therapeutic drugs that diffuse, decay, and are consumed by agents. 4.3.3 Interaction and Behavior Rules Rules define how each cell behaves and makes decisions at every step of the simulation. Some examples include: Movement: Random walks, contact-inhibited crawling, or chemotaxis toward nutrient sources. Feeding & Metabolism: Extracting energy from the local environment or prey to fuel baseline basal metabolic costs. Immune Attacks (Predation): Immune cells spotting cancer cells upon physical proximity, causing them to lock onto them and destroy them (cell lysis). Reproduction (Proliferation): Dividing into daughter cells when internal energy exceeds a threshold and space is available. Cell Death (Apoptosis): Cell death triggered by starvation (energy dropping below zero), immune destruction, or senescence. 4.3.4 Iterative Scheduling Loop Time advances in discrete increments (\(\Delta t\)). At each time step: Activation Order: Living agents are activated. In asynchronous scheduling, the order is randomized at every step to prevent execution order artifacts. Action Execution: Each agent evaluates its local neighborhood, updates its energy, moves, interacts, and potentially reproduces or dies. Environmental Update: Diffusive fields diffuse/decay and renewable resources regenerate. State Census: Macroscopic summary statistics (e.g., total population counts, spatial clustering) are logged for analysis. 4.4 Hands-On Implementation Walkthrough: Tumour-Immune Dynamics in R & Plotly In Chapter 1, we introduced the classic Lotka-Volterra system to describe predator-prey interactions between cytotoxic immune effector cells (\(E\), predators) and tumour cells (\(T\), prey): \[\frac{dT}{dt} = a\, T - b\, T E, \qquad \frac{dE}{dt} = c\, T E - d\, E\] In continuous ordinary differential equations (ODEs), populations are assumed to be “well-mixed” and uniformly distributed across continuous space. However, real clinical tumors grow in complex, structured physical microenvironments where space and local biology govern survival: Spatial Clustering & Nodule Formation: Tumours do not disperse evenly; they originate as dense, localized nodules surrounded by healthy tissue and vascular beds. Contact Inhibition (Volume Exclusion): Cells require physical room to divide. Even if nutrients are abundant, cells tightly packed in the tumor core cannot proliferate until space opens up at the tumor margin. Chemotaxis (Directed Search): Immune cells do not wander blindly. Instead, they sense chemical gradients (chemokines) secreted by tumour cells, migrating preferentially toward cancer nests. T-Cell Exhaustion: Chronic antigenic stimulation causes cytotoxic T cells to become functionally exhausted, losing their ability to kill or proliferate. Therapeutic Rescue (Immunotherapy): Immune checkpoint inhibitors (such as anti-PD-1 / anti-PD-L1 antibodies) block inhibitory pathways, reinvigorating exhausted T cells and restoring immune control. Here, we translate these Lotka-Volterra tumour-immune dynamics into an Agent-Based Model (ABM). They take up nutrients supplied by nearby blood vessels to fuel their basic survival, move into open surrounding areas, and multiply until they run out of room (contact-inhibited growth). If they run out of nutrients and energy (energy drops below zero), they starve and die from necrosis. Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes (\(E\), Predators): These cells patrol the tissue domain. They detect tumor cells via chemotaxis and attack on contact with probability \(p_{\text{kill}}\). Killing a target provides them with energy (target lysis) and triggers them to divide. After sustained killing, T cells reach an exhaustion limit, losing both their ability to kill (cytotoxicity) and their ability to divide (proliferative potential). Vascular Nutrient Field (Resource): A 2D grid representing oxygen and glucose delivery from the capillary microvasculature. Once a tumor cell feeds at a site, the nutrients are depleted and a countdown starts until nearby blood vessels replenish it. Why We Use an R environment (new.env()) In standard R, when you pass a data frame or list into a function, R creates a duplicate copy in memory whenever you modify it (this is called “copy-on-modify”). In an agent-based model where thousands of cells move, eat, and divide across hundreds of time steps, copying the entire world at every tick would make the simulation extremely slow! An R environment (m <- new.env()) acts like a shared notebook or container box. When functions read and update values inside m, they modify the original data directly in place, ensuring our simulation runs at top speed. 4.4.2.2 2. Why We Use “Parallel Vectors” Instead of creating hundreds of separate complex objects for every individual cell, we store agent attributes in synchronized, simple 1D vectors: m$x[i] and m$y[i]: the \((x, y)\) coordinate of cell i. m$type[i]: whether cell i is a tumour cell (1) or a T cell (2). m$energy[i]: the remaining metabolic energy of cell i. m$kills[i]: how many tumour cells T cell i has eliminated. m$alive[i]: TRUE if the cell is currently living, FALSE if dead. For example, cell number \(7\) is described simply by looking at index \(7\) across all vectors: its position is (m$x[7], m$y[7]) and its energy is m$energy[7]. 4.4.2.3 3. Spatial Matrix for Volume Exclusion To enforce contact inhibition (at most one tumour cell per site), we maintain a 2D integer matrix m$tum. If coordinate \((x, y)\) is empty, m$tum[x, y] == 0. If occupied, it holds the ID number of that tumour cell. 4.4.2.4 4. The Moore 8-Neighborhood & Periodic Boundary Wrapping Cells can move or divide into any of their \(8\) surrounding neighbors (North, South, East, West, and the 4 diagonals): (-1, -1) ( 0, -1) ( 1, -1) (-1, 0) [ Cell ] ( 1, 0) (-1, 1) ( 0, 1) ( 1, 1) To prevent cells from “falling off” the edge of the tissue grid, we use periodic (toroidal) boundary conditions: a cell that walks off the right edge wraps around to the left edge, and a cell walking off the top wraps to the bottom. In R’s 1-based indexing, this wrap-around is computed cleanly with the modulo operator: wrapped_x <- ((current_x - 1 + dx) %% grid_width) + 1 4.4.3 Code Walkthrough Let us now build the complete agent-based model step-by-step. 4.4.3.1 Step 1: Libraries and Biological Constants We load plotly and define our integer identifiers and neighborhood step offsets. library(plotly) # Numerical labels for our cell types TUMOUR <- 1L # 1 represents a tumour cell (prey) TCELL <- 2L # 2 represents a cytotoxic T lymphocyte (predator) # Moore 8-neighbourhood coordinate offsets (dx and dy for all 8 surrounding patches) DX <- c(-1L, 0L, 1L, -1L, 1L, -1L, 0L, 1L) DY <- c(-1L, -1L, -1L, 0L, 0L, 1L, 1L, 1L) # Bundle default parameters into a clean, reusable list default_params <- list( dims = 40, # 40x40 spatial lattice (1,600 patches) n_tumour = 60, # Initial tumour cell count n_tcell = 10, # Initial patrolling T-cell count resupply_time = 12, # Steps for depleted nutrient to replenish de_tumour = 14, # Energy gained by tumour from nutrient tumour_div = 0.06, # Tumour division probability per step tumour_motility = 0.05, # Tumour migration probability per step de_tcell = 12, # Energy gained by T cell per tumour kill p_kill = 0.50, # Base kill probability on contact tcell_prolif = 0.40, # Clonal expansion probability after kill exhaustion_limit = 6, # Kills before T cell becomes exhausted recruit = 1.0, # T-cell recruitment rate per 100 tumour cells chemotaxis = 0.60, # Chemotactic bias toward neighbouring tumour therapy = FALSE, # Checkpoint inhibitor therapy active? therapy_start = 200, # Step at which therapy is initiated therapy_kill_boost = 1.6, # Multiplier for kill probability under therapy therapy_exh_mult = 4, # Multiplier for exhaustion limit under therapy seed = 1 # Random seed for reproducible results ) 4.4.3.2 Step 2: Initializing the Model Environment The initialize_model() function builds the tissue lattice, seeds the central tumor nodule, places patrolling T cells, and sets up the vascular nutrient grid. initialize_model <- function(p = default_params) { set.seed(p$seed) # Fix seed for reproducible scientific simulations m <- new.env() # Create our mutable simulation environment W <- H <- as.integer(p$dims) m$W <- W m$H <- H m$p <- p # --- Seed the Central Tumour Nodule --- # In vivo tumors originate as compact masses. # To mimic this, we calculate each lattice site's distance from the center, add a small amount of random noise, # and pick the nearest sites to form a naturally rounded cluster. cx <- (W + 1) / 2 cy <- (H + 1) / 2 all_sites <- expand.grid(x = seq_len(W), y = seq_len(H)) distances <- sqrt((all_sites$x - cx)^2 + (all_sites$y - cy)^2) ordered_sites <- all_sites[order(distances + runif(nrow(all_sites), 0, 0.5)), ] nt <- min(p$n_tumour, W * H) tx <- ordered_sites$x[seq_len(nt)] ty <- ordered_sites$y[seq_len(nt)] # --- Seed Patrolling T Cells --- # T cells begin scattered randomly across the tissue microenvironment ncel <- p$n_tcell n_total <- nt + ncel # --- Populate Parallel Attribute Vectors --- m$type <- c(rep(TUMOUR, nt), rep(TCELL, ncel)) m$x <- c(tx, sample.int(W, ncel, replace = TRUE)) m$y <- c(ty, sample.int(H, ncel, replace = TRUE)) m$energy <- as.numeric(c( sample.int(2 * p$de_tumour, nt, replace = TRUE) - 1, sample.int(2 * p$de_tcell, ncel, replace = TRUE) - 1 )) m$kills <- integer(n_total) # Cumulative kills per agent (tracks exhaustion) m$alive <- rep(TRUE, n_total) # Life status: TRUE = active, FALSE = removed # --- Spatial Matrix (Volume Exclusion) --- # Holds the agent ID of the occupying tumour cell, or 0 if vacant m$tum <- matrix(0L, W, H) m$tum[cbind(tx, ty)] <- seq_len(nt) # --- Vascular Nutrient Field --- # TRUE = nutrient patch available; countdown = remaining steps until replenishment m$fully <- matrix(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), W * H, replace = TRUE), W, H) m$countdown <- matrix( ifelse(m$fully, p$resupply_time, sample.int(p$resupply_time, W * H, replace = TRUE) - 1L), W, H ) # History tracking vectors for population time series m$step <- 0L m$kill_events <- 0L m$h_step <- integer(0) m$h_tumour <- integer(0) m$h_active <- integer(0) m$h_exhausted <- integer(0) m$h_nutrient <- integer(0) record(m) # Take initial census m } 4.4.3.3 Step 3: Helper Functions (Adding, Removing, and Finding Neighbors) These concise helper functions manage agent lifecycle changes, boundary math, and therapy state. # Check whether checkpoint inhibitor therapy is active at the current step therapy_on <- function(m) { m$p$therapy && m$step >= m$p$therapy_start } # Dynamic exhaustion threshold (expanded when immunotherapy is active) exh_limit <- function(m) { m$p$exhaustion_limit * (if (therapy_on(m)) m$p$therapy_exh_mult else 1) } # Dynamic kill probability (boosted when immunotherapy is active) kill_prob <- function(m) { min(1.0, m$p$p_kill * (if (therapy_on(m)) m$p$therapy_kill_boost else 1)) } # Add a newborn daughter cell or newly recruited T cell to our parallel vectors add_agent <- function(m, type, x, y, energy, kills = 0L) { m$type <- c(m$type, type) m$x <- c(m$x, x) m$y <- c(m$y, y) m$energy <- c(m$energy, energy) m$kills <- c(m$kills, kills) m$alive <- c(m$alive, TRUE) new_id <- length(m$alive) if (type == TUMOUR) m$tum[x, y] <- new_id new_id } # Mark a cell as dead and clear its coordinate in the spatial matrix remove_agent <- function(m, i) { m$alive[i] <- FALSE if (m$type[i] == TUMOUR) m$tum[m$x[i], m$y[i]] <- 0L } # Calculate the coordinates of all 8 neighbors with toroidal boundary wrap-around neighbours <- function(m, i) { list( x = ((m$x[i] - 1L + DX) %% m$W) + 1L, y = ((m$y[i] - 1L + DY) %% m$H) + 1L ) } 4.4.3.4 Step 4: Tumour Cell Behavior Rules At each time step, every living tumour cell follows four biological rules: Motility: With probability tumour_motility, it migrates into an unoccupied adjacent patch. Basal Metabolism: It consumes \(1\) unit of energy. If its energy drops below zero, it undergoes necrotic cell death from starvation. Nutrient Uptake: If glucose/oxygen is present at its patch, it takes up the nutrient and gains energy (de_tumour). Contact-Inhibited Proliferation: With probability tumour_div, it divides into an empty adjacent patch, splitting its energy with the daughter cell. If all \(8\) neighboring sites are occupied by other cancer cells, division is physically blocked (contact inhibition). tumour_step <- function(m, i) { p <- m$p nb <- neighbours(m, i) # Identify which of the 8 neighbouring lattice sites are unoccupied free <- m$tum[cbind(nb$x, nb$y)] == 0L # 1. Migration: crawl to an empty neighboring patch if (any(free) && runif(1) < p$tumour_motility) { k <- which(free) k <- k[sample.int(length(k), 1)] # Choose one empty neighbor at random m$tum[m$x[i], m$y[i]] <- 0L # Clear old position m$x[i] <- nb$x[k]; m$y[i] <- nb$y[k] # Update coordinates m$tum[m$x[i], m$y[i]] <- i # Register new position # Re-evaluate empty neighbors after moving nb <- neighbours(m, i) free <- m$tum[cbind(nb$x, nb$y)] == 0L } # 2. Basal Metabolism: expend 1 energy unit for survival m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] - 1 if (m$energy[i] < 0) { remove_agent(m, i) # Starvation: cell undergoes necrosis return(invisible()) } # 3. Nutrient Uptake: feed on vascular glucose/oxygen if (m$fully[m$x[i], m$y[i]]) { m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] + p$de_tumour m$fully[m$x[i], m$y[i]] <- FALSE # Nutrient patch is now depleted } # 4. Proliferation: divide into a free neighboring site (contact-inhibited) if (any(free) && runif(1) <= p$tumour_div) { k <- which(free) k <- k[sample.int(length(k), 1)] m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] / 2 # Parent divides energy equally with daughter cell add_agent(m, TUMOUR, nb$x[k], nb$y[k], m$energy[i]) } } 4.4.3.5 Step 5: Cytotoxic T Cell Behavior Rules Each living T cell acts as a patrolling predator: Chemotaxis & Movement: The T cell evaluates its \(8\) neighboring patches. If any neighbor holds a tumour cell, it steps toward it with probability chemotaxis (chemokine gradient guidance); otherwise, it performs a random walk step. Metabolism & Finite Lifespan: The T cell loses \(1\) energy unit per step. If energy drops below zero, it dies of senescence. Exhaustion Check: If the T cell’s cumulative kill count reaches exhaustion_limit, it becomes exhausted: it remains physically present in the tissue but can no longer attack or proliferate. Contact Cytotoxicity: If active (non-exhausted) and sharing a patch with a tumour cell, it attacks with probability kill_prob, destroying the tumour cell (cell lysis), gaining energy (de_tcell), and logging a kill. Clonal Expansion: Following a kill, with probability tcell_prolif, the T cell divides into two active daughter T cells. tcell_step <- function(m, i) { p <- m$p nb <- neighbours(m, i) # 1. Chemotaxis: sense nearby tumour cells and step toward them nearby_tumours <- which(m$tum[cbind(nb$x, nb$y)] > 0L) k <- if (length(nearby_tumours) > 0 && runif(1) < p$chemotaxis) { nearby_tumours[sample.int(length(nearby_tumours), 1)] # Directed step toward tumor } else { sample.int(8L, 1) # Random exploration step } m$x[i] <- nb$x[k] m$y[i] <- nb$y[k] # 2. Metabolism & Natural Lifespan m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] - 1 if (m$energy[i] < 0) { remove_agent(m, i) # T cell dies of natural senescence return(invisible()) } # 3. Exhaustion Check: exhausted T cells cannot kill or proliferate if (m$kills[i] >= exh_limit(m)) { return(invisible()) } # 4. Contact Cytotoxicity: attack tumour cell at current site target <- m$tum[m$x[i], m$y[i]] if (target > 0L && runif(1) <= kill_prob(m)) { remove_agent(m, target) # Lyse the tumour cell m$kill_events <- m$kill_events + 1L m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] + p$de_tcell m$kills[i] <- m$kills[i] + 1L # 5. Clonal Proliferation: divide following antigenic stimulation if (runif(1) <= p$tcell_prolif) { m$energy[i] <- m$energy[i] / 2 # Parent splits energy with daughter T cell add_agent(m, TCELL, m$x[i], m$y[i], m$energy[i], m$kills[i]) } } } 4.4.3.6 Step 6: Environmental Regeneration and Systemic Recruitment Between cellular actions, vascular nutrients replenish and new immune cells enter the tissue from systemic circulation in proportion to tumour antigen load: # Nutrient Regrowth: Depleted vascular patches count down and replenish nutrient_step <- function(m) { R <- m$p$resupply_time growing <- !m$fully ready <- growing & m$countdown <= 0 m$fully[ready] <- TRUE m$countdown[ready] <- R dec <- growing & !ready m$countdown[dec] <- m$countdown[dec] - 1L } # Systemic T-Cell Recruitment: # Bloodborne T cells extravasate into tissue at a rate proportional to tumour antigen load. # The number of new cells arriving each step is sampled from a Poisson distribution. recruit_tcells <- function(m) { n_tum <- sum(m$alive & m$type == TUMOUR) n_new <- rpois(1, m$p$recruit * n_tum / 100) for (j in seq_len(n_new)) { add_agent( m, TCELL, sample.int(m$W, 1), sample.int(m$H, 1), sample.int(2 * m$p$de_tcell, 1) - 1 ) } } # Census function: tallies active, exhausted, and tumour populations counts <- function(m) { a <- m$alive tc <- a & m$type == TCELL exh <- tc & (m$kills >= exh_limit(m)) c( tumour = sum(a & m$type == TUMOUR), active = sum(tc & !exh), exhausted = sum(exh), nutrient = sum(m$fully) ) } # History logger for time-series trajectories record <- function(m) { cc <- counts(m) m$h_step <- c(m$h_step, m$step) m$h_tumour <- c(m$h_tumour, cc[["tumour"]]) m$h_active <- c(m$h_active, cc[["active"]]) m$h_exhausted <- c(m$h_exhausted, cc[["exhausted"]]) m$h_nutrient <- c(m$h_nutrient, cc[["nutrient"]]) } 4.4.3.7 Step 7: The Master Scheduling Loop At each discrete simulation step (\(\Delta t\)), living agents are activated. Notice that we randomly shuffle the execution order (sample.int(...)) so that no individual cell receives an unfair “first-move” advantage at every turn: model_step <- function(m) { # Asynchronous random scheduling: shuffle living agent indices ids <- which(m$alive) ids <- ids[sample.int(length(ids))] for (i in ids) { if (!m$alive[i]) next if (m$type[i] == TUMOUR) tumour_step(m, i) else tcell_step(m, i) } nutrient_step(m) # Regenerate depleted vascular nutrients recruit_tcells(m) # Recruit circulating T cells based on tumour antigen load m$step <- m$step + 1L record(m) # Record population census # Housekeeping: periodically prune dead agents from memory so vectors stay compact if (length(m$alive) > 4 * sum(m$alive) + 500) { keep <- m$alive old_ids <- which(keep) for (v in c("type", "x", "y", "energy", "kills", "alive")) m[[v]] <- m[[v]][keep] remap <- integer(length(keep)) remap[old_ids] <- seq_along(old_ids) m$tum[m$tum > 0L] <- remap[m$tum[m$tum > 0L]] } } 4.4.4 Interactive Visualizations with Plotly 4.4.4.1 1. Chapter 5 Optimal Control Mathematical models of cancer describe how tumor populations evolve over time and how they interact with the immune system, treatment, and their surrounding environment. While these models can provide insight into tumor dynamics and treatment response, they often assume that treatment is prescribed according to a fixed schedule. Optimal control theory extends this framework by treating therapy as a time-dependent decision variable. Rather than simply predicting tumor evolution under a prescribed treatment, we seek a treatment strategy that optimizes a specified therapeutic objective. In cancer modeling, this objective typically involves balancing tumor reduction against treatment-related toxicity, drug consumption, or damage to healthy tissue. The resulting mathematical problem combines a system of differential equations describing tumor dynamics with an objective functional measuring the performance of a treatment strategy. Optimal control has been applied to several cancer treatment problems, including chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and combination therapy. Examples include studies of competing chemotherapy strategies, immune-mediated tumor dynamics, and treatment optimization in the presence of drug resistance (Fister and Panetta 2003; de Pillis and Radunskaya 2001; de Pillis et al. 2006; Carrère 2017). This chapter introduces the mathematical foundations of optimal control for ordinary differential equation (ODE) models of cancer. We begin with the general formulation of an optimal control problem, followed by Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle and the derivation of the associated optimality system. A Gompertzian tumor-growth model is then used to illustrate the derivation and numerical solution of an optimal treatment strategy using the forward–backward sweep method. Throughout the chapter, each new concept is followed by an example for a second model: a simplified version of the tumor–immune model of Kuznetsov et al. (1994), presented in Section 3.1, in which the tumor has no carrying capacity. The examples are numbered within the chapter, separately from the definitions and theorems. 5.1 Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem An optimal control problem consists of three main components: A dynamical system describing the evolution of the state variables. A set of admissible controls representing the allowable interventions. An objective functional measuring the performance of different control strategies. 5.1.1 State equations, controls, and objective Let \(x(t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) denote the state vector, which may include tumor cells, immune effector cells, and drug concentrations, and let \(u(t)\in\mathbb{R}^m\) denote the treatment input, such as a chemotherapy infusion rate, a drug dose, or an immunotherapy input. Treatment is subject to clinical limits, so at each time the control takes values in a set \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) of allowed treatment levels. For a single treatment input a common choice is \(U=[0,M]\), where \(M\) is the maximum allowable treatment intensity. Example 5.1 (Simplified Kuznetsov model) We use the Kuznetsov model of Section 3.1 in the dimensionless form (3.4)–(3.5) of Section 3.4, without immune resistance. One unit of \(E\) or \(T\) is \(10^6\) cells, and one unit of time is \(1/(n\cdot10^6)\approx 9.1\) days, with \(n\) from Table 3.1. We remove the carrying capacity of the tumor (\(b=0\)), so that without immune killing the tumor grows exponentially, and add chemotherapy with intensity \(u(t)\): \[\begin{aligned} E'&=s+\frac{p\,E\,T}{g+T}-m\,E\,T-d\,E, &\qquad E(0)&=E_0,\\ T'&=a\,T-E\,T-\delta\,u(t)\,T, &\qquad T(0)&=T_0. \end{aligned}\] The parameters \(s\), \(p\), \(g\), \(m\), \(d\), and \(a\) have the meanings and dimensionless values of Table 3.2. The new term \(-\delta uT\) is the killing of tumor cells by the drug, at rate \(\delta\) per unit of treatment intensity. The state is \(x=(E,T)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^2\) and the control is scalar. The values used for treatment, cost, and initial conditions are listed in Table 5.1. Table 5.1: Treatment, cost, and initial values for the Kuznetsov example. Definition 5.1 (Admissible Controls) Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) represent the set of allowable control values. The set of admissible controls is \[\mathcal{U} = \left\{ u:[0,t_f]\rightarrow U \mid u \text{ is Lebesgue measurable} \right\}.\] For a scalar control with \(U=[0,M]\), the admissible controls satisfy \[0\leq u(t)\leq M\] for almost every \(t\in[0,t_f]\). Example 5.2 (Admissible chemotherapy schedules) In Example 5.1 the treatment intensity is measured as a fraction of the maximum tolerated dose, so \(U=[0,M]\) with \(M=1\). Every measurable schedule with values in \([0,1]\) is admissible. In particular, the ON–OFF schedule that gives the full dose for a time \(\tau_{\mathrm{on}}\) and then pauses for a time \(\tau_{\mathrm{off}}\), \[u_{\tau_{\mathrm{off}}}(t)= \begin{cases} M, & \text{if } t-k(\tau_{\mathrm{on}}+\tau_{\mathrm{off}})\in[0,\tau_{\mathrm{on}}) \text{ for some integer } k\geq0,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases}\] is piecewise constant, hence measurable, and therefore admissible. Continuous treatment at full dose is the case \(\tau_{\mathrm{off}}=0\). Section 5.5 compares these schedules with the optimal control. Definition 5.2 (Optimal Control Problem) Given the functions \[g:[0,t_f]\times\mathbb{R}^n\times U \rightarrow\mathbb{R}^n,\] \[f:[0,t_f]\times\mathbb{R}^n\times U \rightarrow\mathbb{R},\] and \[\phi:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\] the optimal control problem is to minimize \[J(u) = \int_0^{t_f} f(t,x(t),u(t))\,dt + \phi(x(t_f))\] over all \(u\in\mathcal{U}\), subject to the state equations \[x'(t)=g(t,x(t),u(t)), \qquad x(0)=x_0, \qquad 0\leq t\leq t_f.\] Here, \(f\) is the running cost, \(\phi\) is the terminal cost, and \(J\) is the objective functional. For each admissible control \(u\), the corresponding solution \(x=x(u)\) is called the associated state. Example 5.3 (An optimal control problem for the Kuznetsov model) For Example 5.1 we take \[J(u)=\int_0^{t_f}\Bigl(A\,T(t)+\frac{B}{2}\,u(t)^2\Bigr)\,dt,\] so that the running cost is \(f(t,x,u)=A\,T+\tfrac{B}{2}u^2\) and the terminal cost is \(\phi=0\). The first term is the accumulated tumor burden and the second the accumulated burden of treatment. The problem is to minimize \(J\) over \(u\in\mathcal{U}\) subject to the state equations of Example 5.1, with the values of Table 5.1. Definition 5.3 (Optimal Control and Optimal State) An admissible control \(u^*\in\mathcal{U}\) is an optimal control if \(J(u^*)\) is finite and \[J(u^*)\leq J(u) \qquad \text{for all }u\in\mathcal{U}.\] The corresponding state \(x^*=x(u^*)\) is called the optimal state, and the pair \((x^*,u^*)\) is called an optimal pair. Example 5.4 (The optimal control as a benchmark) Since every ON–OFF schedule of Example 5.2 is admissible, Definition 5.3 gives \[J(u^*)\leq J(u_{\tau_{\mathrm{off}}})\qquad\text{for every }\tau_{\mathrm{off}}\geq0 .\] The optimal control is therefore a benchmark for simpler clinical schedules: no ON–OFF schedule, whatever its pause, can do better. Section 5.5 computes \(u^*\) and measures how far ON–OFF schedules are from it. 5.1.2 Components of the objective functional In cancer models, the running cost may penalize tumor burden, treatment intensity, or other undesirable outcomes. A terminal cost can additionally penalize the remaining tumor population at the end of the treatment period. Some commonly used terms are summarized in Table 5.2. Table 5.2: Common components of objective functionals in cancer treatment models. Term Interpretation Comment \(A\,T(t)\) or \(A\,T(t)^2\) Tumor burden The quadratic term penalizes larger tumor populations more heavily. \(\frac{B}{2}u(t)^2\) Treatment intensity Penalizes high treatment intensities and produces a strictly convex quadratic control cost. \(B\,u(t)\) Drug consumption Penalizes cumulative drug delivery and may lead to bang-bang or singular controls. \(-C\,E(t)\) Immune response Rewards larger immune effector populations. \(C\,T(t_f)\) Terminal tumor burden Penalizes the remaining tumor population at the end of treatment. The coefficients \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) determine the relative importance of the different components of the objective functional. Their appropriate values depend on the model, the scaling of the state variables, and the therapeutic objectives. Consequently, they should be interpreted in the context of the particular application, and sensitivity to their values should be examined. Example 5.5 (Choosing the weights) The objective functional of Example 5.3 uses the tumor-burden term \(A\,T\) and the quadratic treatment term of Table 5.2. Because \(T\) is measured in units of \(10^6\) cells and \(u\) is a fraction of the maximum dose, the weights must be read on these scales. With \(A=1\) and \(B=50\), one time unit at full dose adds \(B/2=25\) to \(J\), as much as one time unit with a tumor of 25 units (\(2.5\times10^7\) cells). Adding \(-C\,E\) would reward schedules that preserve the immune response, and adding \(C\,T(t_f)\) would penalize the tumor left at the end of treatment. 5.1.3 Why use a quadratic treatment cost? A quadratic treatment cost is frequently used in optimal control models of cancer. For example, including a term \(Bu(t)^2/2\) penalizes high treatment intensities more heavily than low ones. This can represent the increasing burden associated with intensive treatment. The quadratic formulation also has a mathematical advantage: it produces a strictly convex Hamiltonian with respect to the control when \(B>0\) and the remaining dynamics are affine in \(u\). Consequently, the unconstrained optimal control can often be obtained explicitly and then restricted to its admissible interval. In contrast, a linear treatment cost may produce bang-bang controls, in which treatment switches between its minimum and maximum allowable levels. Singular controls may also arise and require additional analysis (Lenhart and Workman 2007; Schättler and Ledzewicz 2015). Example 5.6 (Linear treatment cost and ON--OFF control) If the treatment term in Example 5.3 were \(B\,u\) instead of \(\tfrac{B}{2}u^2\), the Hamiltonian (Example 5.8) would be linear in \(u\), with coefficient \(B-\delta\lambda_T T\). Minimizing it over \([0,M]\) gives the full dose \(u=M\) where \(B-\delta\lambda_TT<0\) and no drug where \(B-\delta\lambda_TT>0\). The optimal treatment is then of ON–OFF type, but its switching times are determined by the adjoint \(\lambda_T\) rather than fixed in advance; a singular arc can occur where \(B-\delta\lambda_TT\) vanishes on an interval. With the quadratic cost, the optimal dose can also take intermediate values. 5.1.4 Existence of an optimal control Theorem 5.1 (Existence of an Optimal Control; Fleming and Rishel) Consider the optimal control problem in Definition 5.2 with \(\phi=0\). Suppose the following conditions hold: The set of admissible controls with corresponding state solutions is nonempty. The control set \(U\) is closed and convex. The function \(g(t,x,u)\) is continuous and affine in the control, so that \[g(t,x,u) = \alpha(t,x)+\beta(t,x)u.\] Furthermore, there exists a constant \(C>0\) such that \[|g(t,x,u)| \leq C(1+|x|+|u|).\] The running cost \(f(t,x,u)\) is convex with respect to \(u\) on \(U\). There exist constants \(c_1>0\), \(c_2\), and \(p>1\) such that \[f(t,x,u) \geq c_1|u|^p-c_2.\] Then there exists an optimal control \(u^*\in\mathcal{U}\) for which \(J(u^*)\) is finite. Theorem 5.1 is a special case of the existence results of Fleming and Rishel (1975). Example 5.7 (Existence for the Kuznetsov problem) Theorem 5.1 applies to the problem of Example 5.3, although the untreated tumor can grow without bound. First, the states stay positive and bounded on \([0,t_f]\) for every admissible \(u\). Writing the tumor equation as \[T(t)=T_0\exp\Bigl(\int_0^t\bigl(a-E(\xi)-\delta u(\xi)\bigr)\,d\xi\Bigr)\] shows that \(T>0\), and \(T(t)\leq T_0e^{a t_f}\) as long as \(E\geq0\). Since \(E'=s>0\) whenever \(E=0\), the effector cells stay positive. Since \(pT/(g+T)<p\) and the terms \(-mET\) and \(-dE\) are nonpositive, \(E'\leq s+pE\), which gives \(E(t)\leq(E_0+s/p)\,e^{p t_f}\). Hence the state equations have a solution on \([0,t_f]\) for every admissible control, so condition 1 holds, and every trajectory stays in a fixed bounded box. The right-hand side may be modified outside a slightly larger box without changing any solution, so the growth bound in condition 3 holds, and it is affine in \(u\) because the control enters only through the term \(-\delta uT\). Finally, \(U=[0,1]\) is closed and convex, \(f=AT+\tfrac{B}{2}u^2\) is convex in \(u\), and \(f\geq\tfrac{B}{2}|u|^2\) because \(T\geq0\), so condition 5 holds with exponent 2. Hence an optimal control exists. 5.2 Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle 5.2.1 The Hamiltonian and adjoint equations Definition 5.4 (Hamiltonian) The Hamiltonian associated with the optimal control problem in Definition 5.2 is \[H(t,x,u,\lambda) = f(t,x,u)+\lambda^\top g(t,x,u).\] Equivalently, \[H(t,x,u,\lambda) = f(t,x,u) + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i g_i(t,x,u),\] where \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is the vector of adjoint variables, also called costate variables. Example 5.8 (Hamiltonian for the Kuznetsov problem) With adjoint variables \(\lambda=(\lambda_E,\lambda_T)^\top\), the Hamiltonian of Example 5.3 is \[H=A\,T+\frac{B}{2}u^2+\lambda_E\Bigl(s+\frac{pET}{g+T}-mET-dE\Bigr)+\lambda_T\bigl(aT-ET-\delta uT\bigr).\] Theorem 5.2 (Pontryagin's Maximum Principle) Suppose \(u^*\) is an optimal admissible control and \(x^*\) is its corresponding state trajectory. Under the standard differentiability and regularity assumptions for the normal case, there exists an absolutely continuous adjoint vector \(\lambda(t)\) satisfying the following necessary conditions. State equations: \[x^{*\prime}(t) = \frac{\partial H}{\partial\lambda} (t,x^*,u^*,\lambda), \qquad x^*(0)=x_0.\] Adjoint equations: \[\lambda'(t) = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x} (t,x^*,u^*,\lambda).\] Transversality condition: \[\lambda(t_f) = \nabla_x\phi(x^*(t_f)).\] Hamiltonian minimization condition: \[H(t,x^*,u^*,\lambda) = \min_{v\in U} H(t,x^*,v,\lambda)\] for almost every \(t\in[0,t_f]\). The Maximum Principle is due to Pontryagin et al. (1962); Lenhart and Workman (2007) derive these conditions for problems of the form considered here. Example 5.9 (Adjoint equations for the Kuznetsov problem) Differentiating the Hamiltonian of Example 5.8 with respect to the states, and using \(\frac{\partial}{\partial T}\frac{pET}{g+T}=\frac{pgE}{(g+T)^2}\), gives \[\begin{aligned} \lambda_E'&=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial E}=-\lambda_E\Bigl(\frac{pT}{g+T}-mT-d\Bigr)+\lambda_T\,T,\\ \lambda_T'&=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}=-A-\lambda_E\Bigl(\frac{pgE}{(g+T)^2}-mE\Bigr)-\lambda_T\bigl(a-E-\delta u\bigr), \end{aligned}\] with the transversality conditions \(\lambda_E(t_f)=\lambda_T(t_f)=0\), since \(\phi=0\). The state equations \(x'=\partial H/\partial\lambda\) are those of Example 5.1. Definition 5.5 (Optimality System) The state equations, the adjoint equations with their transversality conditions, and the characterization of the optimal control obtained from the Hamiltonian minimization condition together form the optimality system. Example 5.10 (Optimality system for the Kuznetsov problem) For the Kuznetsov problem, the optimality system consists of the two state equations of Example 5.1, the two adjoint equations of Example 5.9 with their transversality conditions, and the characterization of \(u^*\) obtained by minimizing the Hamiltonian over \([0,M]\), which is derived in Examples 5.12 and 5.13. The complete system is written out in Example 5.15. 5.2.2 Interpretation of adjoint variables The adjoint variables are also commonly called costates or shadow prices. They describe the marginal effect of changes in the state variables on the optimal objective. Informally, \(\lambda_i(t)\) measures how a small change in the state variable \(x_i(t)\) affects the optimal value of the objective, with the remaining problem appropriately reoptimized. For example, if the tumor adjoint is positive, an increase in tumor burden increases the objective locally. The magnitude of the adjoint helps determine the value of reducing the tumor population through treatment. The biological interpretation of an adjoint variable depends on the objective functional. In particular, an immune-cell adjoint need not have the same sign or interpretation as a tumor-cell adjoint. Example 5.11 (Signs of the Kuznetsov adjoints) In Example 5.9, \(\lambda_T(t)\) is the marginal cost of one additional unit of tumor at time \(t\), and \(\lambda_E(t)\) the marginal cost of one additional unit of effector cells. For the computed solution (Figure 5.4), \(\lambda_E\leq0\) on the whole interval: extra effector cells kill tumor cells and so lower the cost. The tumor adjoint is positive except on the short interval \(8.58\leq t\leq 8.90\), where it is slightly negative (its minimum is \(-0.0021\)). On this interval an additional tumor cell stimulates enough recruitment of effector cells to lower the total cost slightly. The sign of an adjoint must therefore be read from the model, not assumed. 5.2.3 Interior optimal controls When the optimal control lies strictly inside its admissible interval, it must satisfy the first-order optimality condition \[\frac{\partial H}{\partial u}=0.\] For a scalar control, a necessary second-order condition for a local minimum with respect to the control is \[\frac{\partial^2 H}{\partial u^2}\geq 0.\] For multiple controls, the corresponding condition involves the positive semidefiniteness of the Hessian with respect to the control variables. These conditions characterize interior minimizers. When controls are subject to bounds, the minimization must instead be performed over the admissible interval. Example 5.12 (Interior control for the Kuznetsov problem) From the Hamiltonian of Example 5.8, \[\frac{\partial H}{\partial u}=B\,u-\delta\,\lambda_T\,T,\qquad\frac{\partial^2 H}{\partial u^2}=B>0 .\] The Hamiltonian is strictly convex in \(u\), and on any interval where \(0<u^*<M\), \[u^*(t)=\widetilde u(t)=\frac{\delta\,\lambda_T(t)\,T^*(t)}{B}.\] The dose is proportional to \(\lambda_T\,T\), the marginal cost of the tumor multiplied by the number of tumor cells the drug can act on, and inversely proportional to the price \(B\) of treatment. 5.2.4 Bounded optimal controls Consider a scalar control with \(U=[u_{\min},u_{\max}]\), so that \(u_{\min}\leq u(t)\leq u_{\max}\). The pointwise minimization of the Hamiltonian gives the following characterization: \[\begin{cases} u^*(t)=u_{\min}, & \dfrac{\partial H}{\partial u}>0,\\[8pt] u_{\min}<u^*(t)<u_{\max}, & \dfrac{\partial H}{\partial u}=0,\\[8pt] u^*(t)=u_{\max}, & \dfrac{\partial H}{\partial u}<0, \end{cases}\] where \(\partial H/\partial u\) is evaluated at \((t,x^*(t),u^*(t),\lambda(t))\). Equivalently, if \(u^*(t)=u_{\min}\) then \(\partial H/\partial u\geq 0\), and if \(u^*(t)=u_{\max}\) then \(\partial H/\partial u\leq 0\). For a strictly convex quadratic Hamiltonian, solving the first-order condition gives an unconstrained minimizer, denoted by \(\widetilde{u}(t)\). The bounded optimal control is then obtained by projecting this value onto the admissible interval: \[u^*(t)=\min\left\{u_{\max},\,\max\{u_{\min},\widetilde{u}(t)\}\right\}.\] This projection formula is used in the numerical implementations later in the chapter. Example 5.13 (Bounded control for the Kuznetsov problem) With \(U=[0,M]\), the projection formula gives \[u^*(t)=\min\Bigl\{M,\,\max\Bigl\{0,\,\frac{\delta\,\lambda_T(t)\,T^*(t)}{B}\Bigr\}\Bigr\}.\] For the values of Table 5.1, the upper bound is active at the start of treatment: the computed schedule gives the full dose until \(t\approx 0.7\) (about 7 days), after which \(\delta\lambda_TT/B\) falls below \(M\) (Figure 5.4). 5.2.5 Multiple states and multiple controls For a model with \(n\) state variables and \(m\) control variables, there is one adjoint equation for each state variable and one pointwise minimization condition for each control variable. The adjoint equation associated with the state variable \(x_i\) is \[\lambda_i'=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_i}=-\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_j\frac{\partial g_j}{\partial x_i}\right).\] In matrix notation, this becomes \[\lambda'=-\nabla_x f-\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\right)^\top\lambda.\] Thus, the adjoint system depends on the transpose of the Jacobian matrix of the state equations. This relationship is particularly useful when deriving optimality systems for cancer models with several interacting tumor and immune-cell populations. Example 5.14 (Adjoint system in matrix form) For the Kuznetsov problem, \(x=(E,T)^\top\) and \(\nabla_x f=(0,A)^\top\). The Jacobian matrix of the state equations is the Jacobian computed before Proposition 3.1, with \(b=0\) and \(n=1\) and with the drug term \(-\delta u\) added to its last entry, and the matrix form of the adjoint equations reads \[\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_E'\\[4pt] \lambda_T'\end{pmatrix} =-\begin{pmatrix}0\\[4pt] A\end{pmatrix} -\begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{pT}{g+T}-mT-d & -T\\[10pt] \dfrac{pgE}{(g+T)^2}-mE & a-E-\delta u \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}\lambda_E\\[4pt] \lambda_T\end{pmatrix},\] where the matrix is the transpose of the Jacobian. Multiplying out reproduces the adjoint equations of Example 5.9. The transpose moves each interaction into the equation of the other adjoint: the killing of tumor cells by effector cells, which gives the entry \(\partial T'/\partial E=-T\) of the Jacobian, appears as the term \(+\lambda_TT\) in the equation for \(\lambda_E\), and the recruitment of effector cells by the tumor, which gives the entry \(\partial E'/\partial T=pgE/(g+T)^2-mE\), appears in the equation for \(\lambda_T\). Example 5.15 (The complete optimality system) Collecting Examples 5.1, 5.9, and 5.13, the optimality system for the Kuznetsov problem is \[\begin{aligned} E'&=s+\frac{pET}{g+T}-mET-dE,\\ T'&=aT-ET-\delta u^*T,\\ \lambda_E'&=-\lambda_E\Bigl(\frac{pT}{g+T}-mT-d\Bigr)+\lambda_TT,\\ \lambda_T'&=-A-\lambda_E\Bigl(\frac{pgE}{(g+T)^2}-mE\Bigr)-\lambda_T(a-E-\delta u^*),\\ u^*&=\min\Bigl\{M,\,\max\Bigl\{0,\,\frac{\delta\lambda_TT}{B}\Bigr\}\Bigr\}, \end{aligned}\] with \(E(0)=E_0\), \(T(0)=T_0\), and \(\lambda_E(t_f)=\lambda_T(t_f)=0\). The two states run forward from \(t=0\) and the two adjoints run backward from \(t=t_f\); they are coupled through \(u^*\) and through the products \(ET\) and \(\lambda_TT\). 5.2.6 Sufficient conditions Theorem 5.3 (Sufficiency; Mangasarian) Suppose the control set \(U\) is convex, the terminal cost \(\phi\) is convex and differentiable, and an admissible control \(u^*\in\mathcal{U}\) with corresponding state \(x^*\) and an absolutely continuous adjoint vector \(\lambda\) satisfies the state equations, adjoint equations, transversality condition, and Hamiltonian minimization condition. If, for almost every \(t\in[0,t_f]\), the mapping \[(x,u) \mapsto H(t,x,u,\lambda(t))\] is convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\times U\), then \(u^*\) is an optimal control. If the mapping is strictly convex, then \(u^*\) is the unique optimal control. This sufficiency result is due to Mangasarian (1966). Example 5.16 (Sufficiency fails for the Kuznetsov problem) The Hamiltonian of Example 5.8 is affine in \(E\), so \(\partial^2H/\partial E^2=0\), while \[\frac{\partial^2H}{\partial E\,\partial T}=\lambda_E\Bigl(\frac{pg}{(g+T)^2}-m\Bigr)-\lambda_T .\] Whenever this mixed derivative is nonzero, the Hessian of \(H\) with respect to \((E,T)\) has determinant \(-(\partial^2H/\partial E\,\partial T)^2<0\), so \(H\) is not convex in \((x,u)\) and Theorem 5.3 does not apply. Optimality of the computed solution therefore rests on existence (Example 5.7) together with uniqueness of the solution of the optimality system. 5.2.7 Uniqueness Definition 5.6 (Uniqueness of the Optimal Control) An optimal control \(u^*\) is unique if every other optimal control \(u\) satisfies \[u(t)=u^*(t) \qquad \text{for almost every }t\in[0,t_f].\] If the state equations have a unique solution for each admissible control, the corresponding optimal state is also unique. Example 5.17 (Checking uniqueness numerically) Uniqueness of the optimal control is difficult to prove for nonlinear models over long time horizons, and the Kuznetsov problem with \(t_f=20\) is no exception. A practical check is to solve the optimality system from several initial guesses. Starting the safeguarded sweep of Section 5.5.2 from full-dose treatment, half-dose treatment, and the ON–OFF schedules with \(\tau_{\mathrm{on}}=0.5\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{off}}=0.5\) or \(1\) gives the same control and the same value \(J=259.65\) in all four cases. This does not prove uniqueness, but it is reassuring. 5.3 A Gompertzian Tumor-Growth Model To illustrate the derivation and numerical solution of an optimal treatment strategy, consider a tumor population \(N(t)\) that follows Gompertzian growth in the absence of treatment, and let \(u(t)\) represent the intensity of a chemotherapy treatment. The controlled model is \[\frac{dN}{dt}=rN\ln\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)-\delta u(t)N,\qquad N(0)=N_0,\] where \(r>0\) is the tumor growth parameter, \(\delta>0\) represents treatment efficacy, and \(0<N_0<1\). Here, the tumor population is normalized so that the carrying capacity is one. The first term describes Gompertzian tumor growth, while the second represents treatment-induced tumor reduction. Proposition 5.1 (Bounds on the tumor density) For every admissible control \(u\) with \(0\leq u\leq M\), the solution of the Gompertzian model with \(0<N_0<1\) satisfies \(0<N(t)<1\) for all \(t\in[0,t_f]\). Proof. Writing the model as \(N'=N\bigl(r\ln(1/N)-\delta u\bigr)\) gives \[N(t)=N_0\exp\left(\int_0^t\bigl(r\ln(1/N(\xi))-\delta u(\xi)\bigr)\,d\xi\right)>0 .\] Since \(N'\leq rN\ln(1/N)\) and \(N\equiv 1\) is an equilibrium of the untreated equation, the comparison principle gives \(N(t)<1\). We seek a treatment strategy that reduces tumor burden while avoiding unnecessarily intensive chemotherapy. For this purpose, consider the objective functional \[J(u)=\int_0^{t_f}\left[AN(t)^2+u(t)^2\right]dt,\] subject to the state equation and the control constraint \(0\leq u(t)\leq M\). The parameter \(A>0\) determines the relative importance of reducing tumor burden, while the quadratic control term penalizes intensive treatment. There is no terminal cost in this formulation. Therefore, the objective measures tumor burden and treatment intensity over the entire treatment period rather than penalizing only the tumor population at the final time. Theorem 5.1 applies to this problem. Take \(U=[0,M]\). Since \(0<N(t)<1\) for all \(t\) (Proposition 5.1) and \(0\leq N\ln(1/N)\leq e^{-1}\) on \((0,1]\), the right-hand side \(rN\ln(1/N)-\delta uN\) is affine in \(u\) and bounded by \(r/e+\delta M\). The integrand \(AN^2+u^2\) is convex in \(u\) and satisfies \(AN^2+u^2\geq |u|^2\), so condition 5 holds with exponent 2. Hence an optimal control exists. 5.4 Derivation of the Optimality System for the Gompertzian Model and numerical solution 5.4.1 Hamiltonian and adjoint equation Introducing the adjoint variable \(\lambda(t)\), the Hamiltonian is \[H=AN^2+u^2+\lambda\left[rN\ln\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)-\delta uN\right].\] The adjoint equation is obtained from \(\lambda'=-\partial H/\partial N\). Differentiating the Hamiltonian with respect to \(N\) gives \[\frac{\partial H}{\partial N}=2AN+\lambda\left[r\ln\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)-r-\delta u\right].\] Therefore, the adjoint equation is \[\lambda'=-2AN-\lambda\left[r\ln\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)-r-\delta u\right].\] Since the objective functional does not contain a terminal cost, the transversality condition is \(\lambda(t_f)=0\). 5.4.2 Optimal control characterization The optimality condition is obtained by differentiating the Hamiltonian with respect to \(u\): \[\frac{\partial H}{\partial u}=2u-\lambda\delta N.\] For an interior optimal control, \(2u-\lambda\delta N=0\), which gives the unconstrained optimal control \[\widetilde{u}(t)=\frac{\lambda(t)\delta N(t)}{2}.\] Since the treatment intensity is constrained by \(0\leq u(t)\leq M\), the optimal control is \[u^*(t)=\min\left\{M,\,\max\left\{0,\frac{\lambda(t)\delta N(t)}{2}\right\}\right\}.\] The resulting optimality system consists of the state equation, adjoint equation, and optimal control characterization: \[\begin{aligned} N'&=rN\ln\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)-\delta u^*N, & N(0)&=N_0,\\ \lambda'&=-2AN-\lambda\left[r\ln\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)-r-\delta u^*\right], & \lambda(t_f)&=0,\\ u^*&=\min\left\{M,\,\max\left\{0,\frac{\lambda\delta N}{2}\right\}\right\}. \end{aligned}\] The state and adjoint equations are coupled through the optimal control. Moreover, the state has an initial condition, whereas the adjoint has a terminal condition. Consequently, the system forms a two-point boundary value problem. Theorem 5.3 does not apply directly to this problem. Since \(\partial^2\bigl(N\ln(1/N)\bigr)/\partial N^2=-1/N<0\), the Hamiltonian is not convex in \(N\) when \(\lambda>0\). Optimality must therefore be argued through existence, shown in Section 5.3, together with uniqueness of the solution of the optimality system. 5.4.3 The forward–backward sweep method The optimality system is a two-point boundary value problem: the state is specified at the initial time, while the adjoint is specified at the terminal time. The forward–backward sweep method (FBSM) is a numerical approach commonly used to approximate solutions to such systems. It alternates between solving the state equations forward in time and the adjoint equations backward in time, updating the control at each iteration (Lenhart and Workman 2007). A typical implementation consists of the following steps: Discretize the interval \([0,t_f]\) into \(n\) time steps of size \(h=t_f/n\). Choose an initial guess for the control, such as \(u(t)\equiv 0\). Using the current control, solve the state equations forward in time from the initial condition \(x(0)=x_0\). Using the newly computed state trajectory, solve the adjoint equations backward in time from the terminal condition \(\lambda(t_f)\). Update the control using its optimality characterization. For a quadratic control cost, this typically involves projecting the unconstrained control onto its admissible interval. Relax the control update by taking a weighted average of the new and previous control values: \[u_{\mathrm{updated}}=\theta u_{\mathrm{new}}+(1-\theta)u_{\mathrm{old}},\] where \(0<\theta\leq 1\) is a relaxation parameter. Repeat the forward and backward sweeps until the relative changes in the state, adjoint, and control trajectories fall below a prescribed tolerance. The relaxation step can improve numerical stability and convergence in practice. However, convergence of the method is not guaranteed for every model, time horizon, or initial control guess. The choice of time discretization and relaxation parameter can therefore be important. A common convergence criterion is \[\max\left\{\frac{\|u^{(k+1)}-u^{(k)}\|_1}{\max(\|u^{(k+1)}\|_1,\varepsilon)},\frac{\|x^{(k+1)}-x^{(k)}\|_1}{\max(\|x^{(k+1)}\|_1,\varepsilon)},\frac{\|\lambda^{(k+1)}-\lambda^{(k)}\|_1}{\max(\|\lambda^{(k+1)}\|_1,\varepsilon)}\right\}<\mathrm{tol},\] where \(k\) denotes the iteration number, \(\mathrm{tol}\) is the prescribed tolerance, and \(\varepsilon>0\) is a small number used to avoid division by zero. 5.4.4 Implementation in R For the Gompertzian model, the state and adjoint equations are those of the optimality system above. Both equations can be integrated numerically using the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method (RK4). The state equation is integrated forward from \(N(0)=N_0\), while the adjoint equation is integrated backward from \(\lambda(t_f)=0\). At each iteration, the control is updated by the projection formula. The following R implementation illustrates the forward–backward sweep procedure. fbsm <- function(r = 0.3, A = 3, delta = 0.45, N0 = 0.975, M = 1.0, tf = 20, n = 1000, tol = 1e-3, max_iter = 500, theta = 0.5) { h <- tf / n t <- seq(0, tf, length.out = n + 1) u <- numeric(n + 1) N <- numeric(n + 1) lam <- numeric(n + 1) # Right-hand side of the state equation fN <- function(N, u) { r * N * log(1 / N) - delta * u * N } # Right-hand side of the adjoint equation fl <- function(N, lam, u) { -2 * A * N - lam * (r * log(1 / N) - r - delta * u) } eps <- 1e-12 err <- Inf for (it in 1:max_iter) { u_old <- u N_old <- N lam_old <- lam # Forward sweep: state equation (RK4) N[1] <- N0 for (i in 1:n) { um <- 0.5 * (u[i] + u[i + 1]) k1 <- fN(N[i], u[i]) k2 <- fN(N[i] + h * k1 / 2, um) k3 <- fN(N[i] + h * k2 / 2, um) k4 <- fN(N[i] + h * k3, u[i + 1]) N[i + 1] <- N[i] + h / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4) } # Backward sweep: adjoint equation (RK4) lam[n + 1] <- 0 for (i in (n + 1):2) { um <- 0.5 * (u[i] + u[i - 1]) Nm <- 0.5 * (N[i] + N[i - 1]) k1 <- fl(N[i], lam[i], u[i]) k2 <- fl(Nm, lam[i] - h * k1 / 2, um) k3 <- fl(Nm, lam[i] - h * k2 / 2, um) k4 <- fl(N[i - 1], lam[i] - h * k3, u[i - 1]) lam[i - 1] <- lam[i] - h / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4) } # Optimal control update (projection onto [0, M]) u_star <- pmin(M, pmax(0, lam * delta * N / 2)) # Relaxation u <- theta * u_star + (1 - theta) * u_old # Relative convergence error err_u <- sum(abs(u - u_old)) / max(sum(abs(u)), eps) err_N <- sum(abs(N - N_old)) / max(sum(abs(N)), eps) err_lam <- sum(abs(lam - lam_old)) / max(sum(abs(lam)), eps) err <- max(err_u, err_N, err_lam) if (err < tol) break } list(t = t, N = N, u = u, lam = lam, iterations = it, error = err) } The implementation returns the time vector, tumor trajectory, optimal treatment profile, adjoint trajectory, number of iterations, and final convergence error. sol <- fbsm() cat("Iterations:", sol$iterations, " Final error:", signif(sol$error, 3), "\n") Iterations: 9 Final error: 0.000497 op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(sol$t, sol$N, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "Time (days)", ylab = "Tumor density N(t)") plot(sol$t, sol$u, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "Time (days)", ylab = "Treatment u(t)") Figure 5.2: Optimal tumor density and treatment for the Gompertzian model. par(op) The numerical solution should be examined to verify that the control remains within its admissible bounds and that the state and adjoint trajectories satisfy their respective boundary conditions. It is also useful to evaluate the objective functional under the computed treatment strategy and compare it with the objective values obtained under simple alternative strategies, such as no treatment or a constant treatment intensity. Such comparisons provide a practical check on the numerical solution, although they do not independently establish global optimality. 5.4.5 Interactive example The Shiny app app_gompertz.R solves the Gompertzian problem with the forward–backward sweep whenever a slider moves.
